questions.explanation: Concurrency = throughput x latency = 5,000 per second x 0.05 s = 250. The tempting 100,000 comes from dividing by 0.05 instead of multiplying, and 25 comes from treating 50 ms as 0.005 s.

questions.text: Which of these are single points of failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: One Redis instance that holds the sessions for every app server
Four stateless app servers spread across two availability zones
One database primary with no standby or replica
Two load balancers sharing a virtual IP, with automatic failover

questions.explanation: If the only Redis or the only database primary dies, everything that depends on it stops, however many app servers sit in front. Redundant stateless servers and a failover pair of load balancers are the fixes, not the problem.

questions.text: A dashboard shows an average latency of 80 ms and a p99 of 300 ms. What does the p99 figure mean?

options.text: 99% of requests finished in 300 ms or less, and the slowest 1% took longer
The average of the slowest 1% of requests is 300 ms
300 ms is the longest any request has taken
Requests are 99% likely to take exactly 300 ms

questions.explanation: A percentile is a cut-off: p99 is the value that 99% of requests stay under. The tail can be far worse than the cut-off, and the average hides it, which is why latency targets are written as percentiles.

questions.text: Shortening the time it takes to recover from a failure can raise availability as much as making failures less frequent.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Availability is roughly MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), so cutting the repair time raises it just as lengthening the time between failures does. Automated failover that turns a 30-minute outage into 30 seconds is often easier than preventing the failure.

questions.text: If one server handles 1,000 requests per second, 10 servers will always handle 10,000 requests per second.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Scaling is linear only when nothing is shared. A shared database, lock or other serial part caps the gain (Amdahl's Law), so the added servers deliver less than 10x.

tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.title: TCP, DNS, ports and NAT
tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.description: How a name becomes an address, how a connection reaches the right program, and what the failure messages tell you.

questions.text: A client tries to connect to a server's port and gets "Connection refused" almost instantly. What is the most likely situation?

options.text: A firewall is silently dropping the SYN packets
The server's host is powered off
The host is reachable, but nothing is listening on that port
The domain name failed to resolve

questions.explanation: A host with no listening socket on the port answers with a TCP reset, which the client reports at once as refused. A silent drop or a dead host gives no reply, so the client waits and times out; a DNS failure would never get as far as a connection.

questions.text: Seeing many sockets in TIME-WAIT on a busy client is a sign that the application is leaking connections.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: TIME-WAIT is how TCP lets a recently closed connection linger briefly to catch stray packets, and it clears on its own. A growing pile of CLOSE-WAIT is the one that usually points to an application that forgets to close sockets.

questions.text: A service answers curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 on its own machine, but other hosts cannot connect. Which explanation and check fit best?

options.text: It is bound to 127.0.0.1 only; ss -tlnp shows 127.0.0.1:8080 instead of 0.0.0.0:8080
TCP does not allow more than one client per port; ss -tan shows the active client
Port 8080 is a privileged port; ls -l shows who owns the binary
The DNS TTL is too long; dig +trace shows the delay

questions.explanation: A socket bound to the loopback address is invisible to every other host, and ss -tlnp shows the address it is bound to. One listening port serves many clients, 8080 is not below 1024, and DNS is not involved when the address is already known.

questions.text: dig example.com returns the correct IP, but curl example.com connects to a different machine. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the TCP three-way handshake is being retransmitted
Whether the server certificate has expired
Whether the DNS record is a CNAME or an A record
Whether /etc/hosts has an entry for that name

questions.explanation: Applications resolve names through the system resolver, which normally reads /etc/hosts before asking DNS, while dig always queries a DNS server. When dig and getent or curl disagree, a hosts-file override is the first suspect.

questions.text: Which statements about DNS are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CNAME record maps a name to another name, which the resolver then looks up
An A record maps a name to an IPv6 address
Lowering a record's TTL before a planned change makes the change take effect sooner
A DNS TTL is a hop counter that routers decrement

questions.explanation: CNAME is an alias, and a short TTL means caches refetch sooner, so operators lower it ahead of a migration. IPv6 addresses live in AAAA records, and the hop counter is the unrelated TTL field in the IP header; a DNS TTL is a caching lifetime in seconds.

questions.text: A host is configured as 10.0.5.40/29. Which of these addresses is on the same local network?
questions.explanation: A /29 has 8 addresses, so blocks start at multiples of 8 and this one spans 10.0.5.40 to 10.0.5.47. 10.0.5.39 and 10.0.5.48 sit in the neighbouring blocks, and 10.0.6.41 is a different third octet entirely, so the host would send those to its gateway.

questions.text: A container on a private address behind NAT can usually open connections to the internet, but an outside host cannot start a connection to it unless a port forward is configured.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NAT creates its translation entry when the inside host sends the first packet out, so replies can find their way back. With no entry and a non-routable private address, unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go until a port forward (destination NAT) maps it.

questions.text: Which workloads fit UDP better than TCP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Transferring a file where every byte must arrive intact
A DNS query and its short response
A database client talking to its server
A live voice call where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: UDP skips the handshake and retransmission, which suits small request/response exchanges and real-time media where timeliness beats completeness. Files and database traffic need TCP's reliable, ordered delivery.

tls-and-https-basics.title: TLS and HTTPS basics
tls-and-https-basics.description: What TLS does and does not protect, how certificates are checked, and where HTTPS ends in a real deployment.

questions.text: Which three guarantees does TLS give an HTTPS connection?

options.text: Compression, caching and load balancing
Encryption, integrity and server authentication
Authorization, rate limiting and logging
Anonymity, availability and data-at-rest protection

questions.explanation: TLS keeps the bytes unreadable to eavesdroppers, detects tampering, and proves the server is who its certificate says. It does not hide who you connected to and does not protect data once it is stored or after TLS ends.

questions.text: If a site presents a valid certificate and the browser shows a padlock, you can be sure the site is honest and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the server is who its certificate says it is. A scam site can have a perfectly valid certificate for its own domain.

questions.text: When a client verifies a server's certificate during the TLS handshake, which checks does it make? Select all that apply.

options.text: The chain of signatures leads up to a root CA in its trust store
The hostname it asked for is covered by the certificate
The website's content has been reviewed and is safe
The current date is inside the certificate's validity period

questions.explanation: Chain of trust, hostname match and validity dates are what the client can actually check. Nothing in the certificate says anything about whether the site's content is safe.

questions.text: All your API clients suddenly fail with "certificate has expired". Which command shows the certificate's validity dates for a host?

options.text: curl -k https://example.com/
dig example.com TXT
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com, piped to openssl x509 -noout -dates
ss -tlnp on the client

questions.explanation: openssl s_client fetches the certificate and x509 -noout -dates prints notBefore and notAfter. curl -k would just skip verification and hide the problem, and the other commands inspect DNS or local sockets.

questions.text: A network observer between a client and an HTTPS site can typically still see which of these? Select all that apply.

options.text: The destination IP address
The value of the Authorization header
The JSON request body
The server name sent in the TLS handshake (SNI), in a typical setup

questions.explanation: TLS hides the HTTP content: headers, cookies, tokens and bodies. It does not hide the fact of the connection, so the IP address and normally the SNI hostname stay visible.

questions.text: TLS is terminated at your load balancer, and the app behind it sees plain http:// requests. How can the app learn that the client originally used HTTPS?

options.text: From an X-Forwarded-Proto header set by the proxy
From the port number on the app's own socket
From the TLS certificate in the request
It cannot be known, so apps must always redirect to HTTPS themselves

questions.explanation: The proxy adds the original scheme as X-Forwarded-Proto, which the app should trust only from a proxy it controls. The certificate and the original TLS session never reach the app once TLS has ended at the balancer.

questions.text: What does the header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 tell a browser?

options.text: The certificate will be renewed automatically in a year
Cookies should be encrypted at rest for a year
Session tokens expire after a year
For the next year, only connect to this site over HTTPS, even if the user types http://

questions.explanation: HSTS makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for the site, which defeats SSL-stripping downgrade attacks. It has nothing to do with certificate renewal or token lifetimes, and it only makes sense once HTTPS works everywhere on the site.

questions.text: Using curl -k (skip certificate verification) inside production code is acceptable because the traffic is still encrypted.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without verification you no longer know who you are talking to, so a man-in-the-middle can present their own certificate and read everything. -k is for debugging a certificate problem only.

tokens-attention-transformers.title: Tokens, attention and transformers
tokens-attention-transformers.description: What a language model actually sees, and the attention mechanics inside a transformer: Q/K/V, scaling, masks and heads.

questions.text: What does a language model actually receive as input?

options.text: The raw characters of the text, one at a time
One ID per word, using a dictionary of every English word
Integer IDs of tokens, which are chunks of text from a fixed learned vocabulary
The text plus a separate list of its grammatical parts

questions.explanation: A tokenizer maps text to vocabulary entries, and the model only sees their integer IDs. A token can be a whole word, a word piece or a single character or byte, so it is not the same as a word.

questions.text: A sentence in Hindi or Japanese usually costs about the same number of tokens as the English sentence with the same meaning.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Tokenizers trained mostly on English text split non-Latin scripts into more, smaller tokens, often 2-3 times as many. That raises both cost and latency for the same content.

questions.text: Why are queries, keys and values computed with three separate learned projections instead of using the token vectors X directly for all three?

options.text: It makes the matrices smaller so attention runs faster
Using X as both query and key forces every token to score highest against itself, which is useless for relating tokens
Softmax only works if the inputs come from a linear projection
It is needed to make the output the same length as the input

questions.explanation: If Q = K = X, the dot product of a vector with itself is always at least as large as with any other vector, so each token is biased toward attending to itself. Separate Wq and Wk remove that guarantee and let the model learn which other tokens matter.

questions.text: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax?

options.text: Dot products grow with the dimension, so large scores would saturate the softmax and leave almost no gradient to learn from
It makes the weights for each row sum to exactly 1
It hides future tokens from the current position
It reduces the number of parameters in the layer

questions.explanation: The spread of dot products between random vectors scales with sqrt(d), so unscaled scores make softmax nearly one-hot and its gradient tiny. Softmax already normalises each row to 1, so that is not the reason for the scaling.

questions.text: A teammate implements a causal mask by setting the scores of future positions to 0 before the softmax. What goes wrong?

options.text: The model crashes with a shape error
Nothing; 0 and -inf give identical weights
Future positions get zero weight, but so do all past positions
Softmax still gives future positions a non-zero weight, so the model quietly leaks information from the future

questions.explanation: A score of 0 is not neutral to softmax; it counts as moderately plausible. Only adding -inf makes exp(-inf) = 0 and gives masked positions exactly zero weight. The bug does not crash, which is why it is dangerous.

questions.text: Going from 1 attention head to 8 heads at the same d_model adds roughly eight times as many parameters.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo stay d_model x d_model whatever the head count. The heads are made by splitting the projected vectors, so the parameter count is unchanged and each head just works in a smaller subspace with its own softmax.

questions.text: Which statements about sampling the next token are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Top-k keeps exactly k candidate tokens, whether the model is confident or torn
Top-p keeps fewer tokens when one token holds most of the probability mass
Temperature removes low-probability tokens from consideration
Greedy decoding samples tokens in proportion to their probabilities

questions.explanation: Top-k is a fixed count while top-p adapts to the shape of the distribution. Temperature only reshapes the probabilities and removes nothing, and greedy decoding always takes the single most likely token rather than sampling.

questions.text: A batch pads shorter sequences with [PAD] tokens so they fit in one tensor. Which are true of masking in this setup? Select all that apply.

options.text: A padding mask stops real tokens from attending to the padding
A padding mask and a causal mask are applied by different mechanisms, so they cannot be combined
Both kinds of mask work by adding -inf to scores before the softmax
A causal mask hides padding tokens, so no padding mask is needed

questions.explanation: Padding masks and causal masks are the same additive -inf tool aimed at different problems: one hides non-content, the other hides the future. They are commonly combined additively before a single softmax. A causal mask hides future positions, which is a different job from hiding padding.

transactions-and-isolation-levels.title: Transactions, isolation and locking
transactions-and-isolation-levels.description: Read anomalies, PostgreSQL's isolation levels, pessimistic and optimistic locking, and how to avoid deadlocks.

questions.text: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and what does each statement see?

options.text: Serializable: every transaction runs as if alone
Repeatable Read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before that statement began
Read Uncommitted: uncommitted changes are visible to everyone

questions.explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but allows a later statement in the same transaction to see newly committed changes. The stronger levels must be requested explicitly.

questions.text: Inside one transaction you run SELECT ... WHERE status = 'open' twice. Between the runs another transaction inserts a matching row and commits, and your second run returns an extra row. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Dirty read
Phantom read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update

questions.explanation: A phantom is a row appearing in (or vanishing from) a set matched by a predicate. A non-repeatable read is when an existing row you already read comes back with a different value. A dirty read involves uncommitted data.

questions.text: On PostgreSQL at Read Committed, an application that reads a balance, adds 10 in code and writes it back is safe from lost updates.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Two transactions can both read 100 and both write back their own result, so the second write overwrites the first. You need row locking, an atomic UPDATE, a version check, or a stronger isolation level with retries.

questions.text: Under PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, two transactions update the same row. The first commits. What happens to the second?

options.text: It fails with a serialization error and must be retried
It silently overwrites the first update
It merges both updates automatically
It keeps waiting until the first transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The second update blocks until the first finishes, then fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' because its snapshot is stale. The application has to catch that error and retry the whole transaction.

questions.text: Which approaches prevent a lost update when many requests change the same account balance? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new balance
An UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? that is retried when it affects 0 rows
A single atomic statement such as UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10
A plain SELECT then UPDATE at Read Committed, with a short transaction

questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking, optimistic versioning and an atomic update each stop two writers from acting on the same stale value. A short transaction narrows the window but does not close it.

questions.text: Two code paths transfer money between accounts A and B. One locks A then B, the other locks B then A, and they occasionally deadlock. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise deadlock_timeout so transactions wait longer
Switch both paths to Read Uncommitted
Add more connections to the pool
Have every code path lock the rows in the same order, such as lowest id first

questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, and a consistent lock order makes a cycle impossible. A longer timeout only delays detection, and PostgreSQL has no real Read Uncommitted anyway.

questions.text: With optimistic locking, your UPDATE ... WHERE id = 'A' AND version = 7 reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?

options.text: The row does not exist, so you should insert it
The database lost the update; you should restart the server
Someone else changed the row first, so re-read it and retry
The write succeeded but nothing needed changing

questions.explanation: The version no longer matches because another transaction bumped it. The application must detect the zero-row result, re-read the fresh row and retry. This only pays off when conflicts are rare.

questions.text: Several workers poll a jobs table, and you want each worker to claim different rows without waiting on each other. Which clause fits?

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... FOR SHARE
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with no other clause
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows another transaction already locked, so workers pick different rows. Plain FOR UPDATE makes every worker queue behind the first, and Serializable would produce errors to retry instead.

client-retries-with-backoff.title: Add retries with backoff to an API client
client-retries-with-backoff.brief:
Your service calls a partner's HTTP API to create shipping labels (`POST /labels`) and to look up their status (`GET /labels/{id}`). Today the client makes one attempt with a 60 second timeout. During busy hours the partner answers some calls with `429 Too Many Requests` (sometimes with a `Retry-After` header), occasionally with `502` or `503`, and a few requests just time out. The first quick fix someone proposed was "retry up to 10 times with no delay", which made an incident worse.

Design the retry behaviour of this client and write it down precisely enough that another engineer could implement it and test it. Pay attention to which calls are safe to repeat: a retried `POST /labels` after a timeout may create two labels if the first attempt actually succeeded. The partner supports an `Idempotency-Key` request header on `POST`.
deliverables: A table of failure types (connection error, timeout, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 400, 401, 404) and whether each is retried, with the reason
The backoff formula with a base delay, a multiplier, a cap and jitter, and which jitter variant you chose and why
How a Retry-After header is honoured and how it combines with your own backoff
The maximum attempts and a total time budget for one logical call, and how this fits inside your own caller's timeout
How you make POST /labels safe to retry (idempotency key: when it is generated, that it is reused across attempts)
Timeouts per attempt (connect and read), and why 60 seconds is too long
A retry budget or circuit breaker so that many clients do not multiply load on a struggling partner
The logging and metrics you would add, and three test cases (including a fake server that fails twice then succeeds)

debug-slow-query-with-explain.title: Debug a slow query with EXPLAIN
debug-slow-query-with-explain.brief:
The "my shipped orders" page of an online shop takes about three seconds and the database CPU spikes when many customers open it. The database is PostgreSQL.

**Schema**

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_key ON customers (email);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
  status      text   NOT NULL,           -- placed, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled
  total_cents integer NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);
-- orders has about 20 million rows; a typical customer has under 200 of them
```

**Query 1 (the page)**

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242 AND status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

```
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
 Limit  (cost=398000.30..398000.35 rows=20 width=48) (actual time=2810.40..2810.45 rows=20 loops=1)
   ->  Sort  (cost=398000.30..398000.60 rows=118 width=48) (actual time=2810.39..2810.42 rows=20 loops=1)
         Sort Key: created_at DESC
         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 28kB
         ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..397600.00 rows=118 width=48) (actual time=1.20..2790.10 rows=96 loops=1)
               Filter: ((customer_id = 4242) AND (status = 'shipped'::text))
               Rows Removed by Filter: 19999904
 Planning Time: 0.15 ms
 Execution Time: 2810.60 ms
```

**Query 2 (support tool, finding a customer by email, case-insensitive)**

```sql
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com';
```

```
 Seq Scan on customers  (cost=0.00..52000.00 rows=5000 width=64) (actual time=0.05..410.30 rows=1 loops=1)
   Filter: (lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'::text)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 999999
 Execution Time: 410.40 ms
```

Diagnose both queries from the plans, propose the fixes, and say how you would prove each fix worked. Assume you are allowed to add indexes, but the table is large and busy.
deliverables: For each query: what the plan shows, in your own words (node types, rows removed by filter, estimated versus actual rows)
The index you would create for query 1, with the column order and the reason for that order (and why the sort node disappears)
The fix for query 2 and why the existing unique index on email cannot be used, plus the trade-off of the fix
The exact CREATE INDEX statements, including how you build them without blocking writes on a busy table
What you expect the new plans to look like and how you would verify it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
Two things that would still make the first query slow after the index exists (for example SELECT * or a very low-selectivity filter) and what you would do about them
How you would check that the new indexes did not hurt write performance, and when ANALYZE matters

paginated-list-endpoint.title: Design a paginated, cache-friendly list endpoint
paginated-list-endpoint.brief:
A blog platform has an endpoint that returns articles:

```
GET /v1/articles?page=3&per_page=20&tag=python
```

It is implemented as `SELECT ... FROM articles WHERE tag = ? ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. The table has 30 million rows and new articles are published every few seconds. Symptoms reported by users and the on-call engineer:

- Deep pages (page 5000 and beyond) take several seconds and load the database.
- A reader scrolling the list sees the same article twice, or misses one, when something new is published between two requests.
- The response is never cached by the CDN because every client sends different query strings and no caching headers are set.
- The endpoint returns a `total` count, and the `COUNT(*)` behind it is the slowest part of the request.

Redesign the endpoint. Write a short design document (and, if you like, a sketch of the handler and the SQL) that fixes all four symptoms without breaking existing clients more than necessary.
deliverables: The new request and response shape, including the cursor parameter and a sample JSON response
What the cursor contains and how it is encoded; why a tie-break column is needed when many rows share the same published_at
The SQL for the first page and for the next page, and the index that makes it fast (column order matters)
What you do about the total count (drop it, estimate it, or return it only on request) and why
Cache-Control, ETag and Vary choices for the first page and for later pages, and what must be part of the cache key
How deletes and edits between two requests behave, and the maximum limit you enforce
A migration path for clients that still send page and per_page

The algorithm (fixed window, sliding window or token bucket) and its numbers
The response when the limit is hit, including the headers a client can use

How you avoid letting an attacker lock a victim out on purpose

zero-downtime-column-migration.title: Plan a zero-downtime column migration
zero-downtime-column-migration.brief:
Your orders table stores the order total as a decimal in a column named `total` (for example `19.99`). It has about 300 million rows and takes writes all day. The team wants to store money as integer cents in a new column `total_cents` and eventually drop `total`.

Constraints:

- The service runs as 12 replicas behind a load balancer and is deployed with a rolling update, so for several minutes old and new versions of the code run at the same time.
- A nightly reporting job, owned by another team, reads `orders.total` directly from a read replica. It cannot change this quarter.
- No maintenance window is allowed. Writes must never fail and no request may see a wrong total.
- The database is PostgreSQL. A plain `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN TYPE` on this table is not acceptable.

Write the migration plan as an ordered runbook. Each step must say whether it is a schema migration, an application deploy, or a data job, what it changes, and what happens if you stop or roll back at that point.
deliverables: The ordered steps using expand and contract: add column, dual-write deploy, backfill, switch reads, stop writing the old column, drop it; for each, the type of step and the rollback
The exact SQL for adding the column and why it is safe on a large table (locks taken and for how long)
The backfill design: batch size, how it walks the table (by primary key range), how it throttles itself, and why it must be idempotent and restartable
How you guarantee rows written during the backfill are correct (the dual-write code, or a trigger as an alternative, and the trade-off between them)
How you verify that total and total_cents agree before switching reads (a query or a checksum, and what you do on a mismatch)
How the reporting job keeps working: when you could finally drop total, what you do if the other team is not ready, and a way to keep total populated for them in the meantime
How and when you add a NOT NULL constraint without a long lock
What you monitor during the migration (replica lag, lock waits, error rate, backfill progress)

questions.q: Explain cache-aside and when you would use it.
questions.a: The application checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache. It is simple, tolerates cache failure, and suits read-heavy data that can be briefly stale.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: When a popular entry expires, many requests miss at once and all hit the database. Prevent it with request coalescing (one rebuild, the rest wait), jittered expiry times, or refreshing early in the background.

questions.q: How do you invalidate a cache correctly?
questions.a: Prefer short TTLs plus explicit invalidation on write. Delete the key after the database write commits. Accept that some staleness is unavoidable and decide how much the data can tolerate.

questions.q: When is caching the wrong answer?
questions.a: When the data must always be current, when the hit rate would be low, or when the slow query should be fixed instead (an index, a better query). A cache hides a problem and adds a consistency problem.

questions.q: How does a B-tree index speed up a query?
questions.a: It keeps keys in sorted order in a balanced tree, so the database finds a value or a range in logarithmic steps instead of reading every row.

questions.q: What is a covering index?
questions.a: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index without reading the table rows.

questions.q: Why might a query ignore an index?
questions.a: The predicate cannot use it (a function on the column, a leading wildcard), the table is small enough that a scan is cheaper, the planner expects most rows to match, or statistics are stale.

questions.q: What is the cost of too many indexes?
questions.a: Every write maintains each index, so inserts and updates slow down, and indexes take memory and disk. Index for the queries you actually run.

questions.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
questions.a: An image is an immutable, layered template containing the filesystem and metadata needed to run an application. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer and isolated process, network and filesystem views. Many containers can run from one image.

questions.q: How does Docker's build cache work and how should that shape your Dockerfile?
questions.a: Each instruction creates a layer that is cached until its inputs change, and a change invalidates every layer after it. So put rarely changing steps first, such as installing dependencies from a lockfile, and frequently changing steps last, such as copying your source code. This makes most rebuilds fast.

questions.q: What is a multi-stage build and why use one?
questions.a: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where a build stage has compilers and tools and the final stage copies only the built artifacts into a small runtime image. It gives smaller images with a smaller attack surface and no build tools or source caches in production.

questions.q: Why should a container run as a non-root user?
questions.a: If the application is compromised, running as root inside the container gives the attacker more power, and a container escape bug would be worse. A dedicated unprivileged user limits the damage. You create the user in the image and make sure files the app needs are readable by it.

questions.q: Why does the exec form of CMD matter for shutdown?
questions.a: In exec form (a JSON array) the application is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly, so it can finish in-flight requests and exit cleanly. In shell form the shell may be PID 1 and not pass the signal on, so the container is killed after the grace period. Your app also needs to handle SIGTERM and stop accepting new work.

questions.q: How should an application receive configuration and secrets in a container?
questions.a: Configuration comes from environment variables or mounted files at runtime, so the same image runs in every environment. Secrets must not be baked into the image or committed to the repository, because image layers keep them; inject them at runtime from a secrets manager or the orchestrator, and restrict who can read them. Note that Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default unless encryption at rest is enabled.

questions.q: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
questions.a: Liveness asks whether the process is broken beyond recovery; failing it makes the platform restart the container, so it should be cheap and not depend on external services. Readiness asks whether the instance can serve traffic now; failing it removes the instance from load balancing without restarting it, so it may check dependencies such as the database. Putting a database check in liveness can cause a restart storm during a database blip.

questions.q: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
questions.a: A rolling update replaces instances gradually, using little extra capacity but mixing old and new versions for a while. Blue-green runs a full second environment and switches traffic at once, giving instant rollback at the cost of double capacity. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and watches metrics before widening, which limits the blast radius of a bad release.

questions.q: What do Kubernetes Deployments, Services and Pods each do?
questions.a: A Pod is the smallest unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage. A Deployment declares how many replicas of a Pod template you want and manages rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives a stable address and load balancing over the Pods that match a label selector, since individual Pod IPs change.

questions.q: Why must database changes be backward compatible during a rolling deploy?
questions.a: During the rollout old and new code run at the same time against the same database, and a rollback puts the old code back. A change that the old version cannot handle, such as dropping or renaming a column, breaks it. The expand and contract pattern solves this: add the new structure first, deploy code that works with both, then remove the old structure later.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter for APIs?
questions.a: An operation is idempotent when doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. Networks fail in the middle of a request, so a client often cannot tell whether the server acted. If the operation is idempotent the client can simply retry.

questions.q: How would you make a POST that charges a card safe to retry?
questions.a: The client sends a unique idempotency key per intended operation. The server stores the key with the result under a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the charge. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result; a concurrent repeat waits or gets a conflict.

questions.q: How long do you keep idempotency keys?
questions.a: Long enough to cover any realistic retry window, commonly 24 hours, then expire them to bound storage. State the window in the API documentation.

questions.q: A retry arrives while the first request is still running. What happens?
questions.a: The unique key makes the second insert fail or block. Either respond 409 so the client retries shortly, or wait for the first to finish and return its result. Never run the work twice.

questions.q: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be safe and to be idempotent?
questions.a: A safe method does not change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). An idempotent method has the same effect on the server whether it is sent once or many times (GET, PUT, DELETE, and also the safe ones). POST is neither by default, which is why a retried POST can create duplicates unless you add an idempotency mechanism.

questions.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
questions.a: PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation you send, and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial change, such as updating one field; whether it is idempotent depends on the operation (setting a field is, appending to a list is not). Use PATCH for partial updates and document what happens to fields you omit.

questions.q: Which status codes would you use for create, validation failure, missing resource, conflict and not authenticated versus not allowed?
questions.a: 201 Created with a Location header for a successful create. 400 for a malformed request, or 422 when the syntax is right but the content fails validation. 404 for a missing resource. 409 for a conflict with current state, such as a duplicate or a version clash. 401 when the caller is not authenticated and 403 when they are authenticated but not permitted.

questions.q: Compare offset pagination and cursor pagination.
questions.a: Offset pagination (page and limit) is simple and allows jumping to a page, but deep offsets are slow because the database still walks the skipped rows, and results shift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. Cursor (keyset) pagination continues from the last item seen using an indexed column, which stays fast and stable on changing data, at the cost of no random page access.

questions.q: How do you make a POST request safe to retry?
questions.a: Have the client send a unique Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the outcome, and if the same key arrives again it returns the stored response instead of repeating the work; a unique constraint makes concurrent duplicates safe. A different request body under the same key should be rejected.

questions.q: How would you version an API, and what counts as a breaking change?
questions.a: Common options are a version in the URL path (/v1/), in a header, or in the media type; the URL is the easiest to understand and route. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) that need no new version. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional input required, or changing semantics are breaking.

questions.q: How do you handle concurrent updates to the same resource through an API?
questions.a: Use optimistic concurrency with an ETag or version number. The client sends it back in If-Match on the update, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed (or 409 with a version field) if the resource changed in the meantime. This prevents the lost update without holding locks across requests.

questions.q: What makes a good error response?
questions.a: A consistent machine-readable shape, such as RFC 9457 problem details, with a stable error code, a human message, and field-level details for validation errors. Use the right status code, include a request or trace id for support, and never leak stack traces or internal details.

questions.q: When would you choose REST, GraphQL or gRPC?
questions.a: REST suits public, resource-oriented APIs and benefits from HTTP caching and tooling. GraphQL helps when many different clients need to choose exactly the fields they want and you want to avoid many round trips, at the cost of harder caching, query-cost control and N+1 care. gRPC suits internal service-to-service calls where a typed contract, streaming and efficiency matter, but browsers need a gateway.

questions.q: How do you design an API to be cache-friendly?
questions.a: Use GET for reads, stable URLs, and Cache-Control with sensible max-age values. Add ETag or Last-Modified so clients can revalidate with a conditional request and receive 304 Not Modified, and use Vary for headers that change the response. Keep personalised data out of shared-cache responses or mark it private.

questions.q: How do you structure a system design interview answer?
questions.a: Clarify requirements first, both functional and non-functional, and state your assumptions. Then estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, go deeper into the one or two components that matter most, and finish with bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs. Keep checking with the interviewer so you spend time where they care.

questions.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
questions.a: Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests the system completes per unit of time. They are related but not the same: adding parallel workers raises throughput without making a single request faster, and batching can raise throughput while increasing latency. Little's law links them: the number of requests in flight equals throughput times average latency.

questions.q: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling.
questions.a: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine; it is simple and needs no code change, but it has a ceiling, costs more per unit at the top end, and leaves one machine as a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds machines behind a load balancer; it scales further and improves availability, but needs stateless services or shared state, and brings distributed-systems problems such as partial failure and consistency.

questions.q: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
questions.a: During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response). When there is no partition you can have both, so CAP is about behaviour under failure, not a permanent choice of two out of three. PACELC extends this by noting that even without a partition there is a trade-off between latency and consistency.

questions.q: How would you calculate availability, and what do "three nines" and "four nines" mean in practice?
questions.a: Availability is uptime divided by total time. 99.9 percent allows roughly 8.8 hours of downtime a year; 99.99 percent allows roughly 53 minutes. Components in series multiply (two 99.9 percent services in a chain give about 99.8 percent), while redundant components in parallel improve it, which is why removing single points of failure matters more than perfecting one component.

questions.q: What is a single point of failure and how do you remove one?
questions.a: A component whose failure takes down the whole system, such as one database, one load balancer or one availability zone. You remove it with redundancy: replicas, multiple instances behind a load balancer, and multiple zones, plus automatic failover that you actually test. Redundancy has a cost and adds complexity, so you apply it where the failure impact justifies it.

questions.q: Why do you want application servers to be stateless?
questions.a: If a server keeps no per-user state in memory, any request can go to any server, so you can add, remove and replace servers freely and failures do not lose sessions. The state moves into shared stores such as a database, cache or token. The trade-off is an extra network hop for that state and the need to make the shared store reliable.

questions.q: Give a back-of-the-envelope estimate for a service with 10 million daily active users, each making 20 requests a day.
questions.a: 10 million times 20 is 200 million requests a day. A day has about 86,400 seconds, so the average is about 2,300 requests per second; assume a peak of two to four times that, around 5,000 to 10,000 per second. The point is the order of magnitude and stating the assumptions, since it tells you whether one database or sharding is needed.

questions.q: How do you justify a trade-off in a design?
questions.a: State the options, the requirement that decides between them, and the cost of the choice. For example, choosing eventual consistency for a feed because users tolerate a few seconds of delay and it buys availability and lower latency, while accepting that a user might briefly not see a new post. Say what would make you change your mind, such as a stricter consistency requirement.

questions.q: When would you choose strong consistency over eventual consistency?
questions.a: When a stale or conflicting read causes real harm: account balances, inventory that must not be oversold, unique usernames, or permission changes. When a stale read is merely a little out of date, such as like counts or a social feed, eventual consistency is usually acceptable and cheaper. Many systems use both in different parts.

questions.q: What do the ACID properties guarantee?
questions.a: Atomicity: a transaction's changes all happen or none do. Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability: once committed, the data survives a crash.

questions.q: Name the common concurrency anomalies.
questions.a: A dirty read sees uncommitted data from another transaction. A non-repeatable read gets different values when reading the same row twice. A phantom read gets different sets of rows when running the same query twice. A lost update happens when two transactions read, modify and write the same row and one overwrites the other. Write skew is when two transactions each read overlapping data and write different rows, together breaking an invariant.

questions.q: What are the standard isolation levels and what is a sensible default?
questions.a: Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable, each preventing more anomalies at higher cost. Read committed is the default in PostgreSQL and a sensible starting point. PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, and its serializable level detects dangerous patterns and may abort a transaction, so the application must be ready to retry.

questions.q: How do you prevent a lost update?
questions.a: Either lock the row while you read and modify it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use optimistic locking with a version column and fail the update if the version changed, or make the change atomic in SQL, such as UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1. The atomic statement is the simplest when it fits the logic.

questions.q: Compare optimistic and pessimistic locking.
questions.a: Pessimistic locking takes locks up front so others wait; it is safe under high contention but reduces concurrency and can deadlock. Optimistic locking does no locking and checks at write time that nothing changed, retrying on conflict; it is cheap when conflicts are rare and wasteful when they are common. Choose by expected contention.

questions.q: What is a deadlock and how do you avoid one?
questions.a: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed; the database detects it and aborts one. Reduce them by locking resources in a consistent order, keeping transactions short, avoiding user interaction or external calls inside a transaction, and retrying the aborted transaction.

questions.q: How would you make "reserve the last seat" correct under concurrency?
questions.a: Make the check and the change one atomic operation: a conditional UPDATE that only succeeds if the seat is still free and checks the affected row count, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction, or a unique constraint on the (show, seat) booking that makes the second insert fail. Never read first and write later without one of those protections.

questions.q: Why should you keep transactions short and avoid network calls inside them?
questions.a: A transaction holds locks and a connection, and in some engines also holds back cleanup of old row versions. A slow call to another service inside it stretches those holds, causes lock waits and connection pool exhaustion, and widens the window for conflicts. Do the slow work outside, and keep the transaction to the database changes that must be atomic.

questions.q: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do and when is it useful?
questions.a: It locks the selected rows and skips rows already locked by other transactions instead of waiting. It is useful for using a table as a job queue: several workers each claim different rows without blocking one another. Be aware it gives up strict ordering and you need a way to handle jobs whose worker died.

questions.q: A payment is committed in your database but the call to the payment provider failed afterwards. How do you keep them consistent?
questions.a: A local database transaction cannot include an external call, so use a pattern that tolerates failure: record the intent in the database first (with an idempotency key), perform the external call, then record the result, with a reconciliation job to resolve anything left unknown. The outbox pattern and sagas with compensating actions are the usual tools.

hld/chat-application.reference:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C1[Client A] <-->|WebSocket| G1[Gateway 1]
  C2[Client B] <-->|WebSocket| G2[Gateway 2]
  G1 --> CS[Chat service]
  G2 --> CS
  CS --> MQ[[Message log per conversation]]
  MQ --> G2
  CS --> DB[(Message store, partitioned by conversation)]
  CS --> R[(Presence + routing: user to gateway)]
  CS --> PUSH[Push for offline users]
```

- Clients hold a **WebSocket** to a gateway; a routing table says which gateway a user is on, so the chat service can deliver to the right one.
- Each conversation is a **partition** with a sequence number, which gives the ordering guarantee; the message is persisted before it is acknowledged.
- Offline users get a **push** notification and fetch history by sequence number on reconnect, which is also how multi-device sync works.
- Presence uses heartbeats with a short TTL in a fast store; do not fan out presence to every contact, only to open chats.
- Large groups use fan-out on read for the message list and fan-out on write only for notifications.

hld/ecommerce-platform.reference:
This is one reasonable design. Decisions with reasonable alternatives are named in the trade-offs.

### Capacity estimate
- Browse: 20 million users x 10 page views = 200 million/day, about 2,300/s average, about 10,000/s at peak (4x). Most are catalog reads, cacheable at the CDN or in a cache.
- Search: perhaps a third of views, so about 3,000/s at peak, served by a search index.
- Orders: 1 million/day is about 12/s average; assume 5x at a busy peak, 60/s. A flash sale at 100x is about 1,200 orders/s overall, but concentrated on a few product rows. That concentration, not the total, is the hard part.
- Order storage: 1 million/day x about 2 KB (header and lines) = 2 GB/day, about 730 GB/year. Easily a sharded relational database.
- Catalog: 50 million products x about 5 KB = 250 GB of metadata, plus images in object storage. Fits a sharded store with a search index beside it.

### Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Shopper] --> CDN[CDN: images, static, cacheable pages]
  CDN --> GW[API gateway]
  GW --> CAT[Catalog service]
  GW --> SRCH[Search service]
  GW --> CART[Cart service]
  GW --> CO[Checkout service]
  CAT --> CDB[(Catalog DB)]
  CAT --> CC[(Cache)]
  SRCH --> ES[(Search index)]
  CDB -. change events .-> ES
  CART --> CR[(Cart store: Redis with DB backup)]
  CO --> INV[Inventory service]
  CO --> ORD[Order service]
  CO --> PAY[Payment service]
  INV --> IDB[(Inventory DB)]
  ORD --> ODB[(Orders DB, sharded by user id)]
  PAY --> PSP[Payment provider]
  PSP -- webhook --> PAY
  ORD --> BUS[[Event bus]]
  BUS --> FUL[Fulfilment]
  BUS --> NOT[Notifications]
  BUS --> ES
```

**Catalog and search (read-heavy).** The catalog database is the source of truth. Changes are published as events and a consumer updates the search index (so search is eventually consistent with the catalog, usually within seconds). Product pages and listings are cached at the CDN and in a cache with short TTLs and invalidation on change. The page shows "in stock" from a cached approximation; the exact check happens at checkout.

**Cart.** A cart is a small document per user (or anonymous cart id) with product id, quantity, and the price seen at add time. Redis with a TTL suits anonymous carts; signed-in carts are persisted to the database so a restart does not lose them. The cart never reserves stock and never decides a price; checkout re-reads the current price.

**Checkout.** The checkout service coordinates, in order: validate the cart and prices, reserve stock, create the order in PENDING, charge, confirm the order. It is a short saga with compensations: if payment fails, release the reservation and mark the order failed.

### Inventory and overselling
Keep available stock in a single row per SKU (and warehouse, if relevant) in a transactional store. Reserve with one conditional statement, so concurrent buyers cannot both take the last unit:

`UPDATE inventory SET available = available - :qty, reserved = reserved + :qty WHERE sku = :sku AND available >= :qty`

If zero rows were updated, the item is out of stock. A reservation record (order id, sku, qty, expires_at) is created in the same transaction. A job releases reservations that expire unpaid (for example after 10 to 15 minutes). On payment success the reservation becomes a sale (reserved decreases, sold is recorded). That sequence means stock is never negative.

**Flash sale.** A single hot row serialises on the row lock, so throughput on one SKU is bounded (often a few hundred to a couple of thousand updates per second per row on a well-tuned database, but treat that as a number to measure, not a promise). Options, from simplest: (1) keep the conditional update but put a queue or waiting room in front, admitting buyers at a rate the row can take; (2) split the stock for a hot SKU into N buckets (for example 20 rows of 50 units), pick a bucket at random and fall through to the next when it is empty, which spreads the contention at the cost of a more complex "is it sold out" check; (3) pre-load the counter into Redis and decrement atomically there, with the database as the durable record and a reconciliation job; this is faster but you must handle Redis loss, so it needs care. Always cap quantity per customer and serve the product page from cache.

### Payment, idempotency and unknown results
- The client creates a checkout attempt and receives a unique idempotency key (or generates one). Every checkout call carries `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores the key with the request fingerprint and the response in a table with a unique constraint; a repeat of the same key returns the stored result, and the same key with a different body is rejected.
- The key is passed on to the payment provider as well, so a retried charge cannot charge twice.
- If the charge call times out, the result is unknown. Do not release the stock and do not retry blindly. Mark the order PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, then resolve it by querying the provider by the idempotency key and by consuming the provider's webhook, whichever arrives first. Webhooks are themselves deduplicated by event id.
- Order state: PENDING -> PAID -> PACKED -> SHIPPED -> DELIVERED, with CANCELLED and REFUNDED branches. Transitions are checked in code and written with a version column to stop concurrent updates winning twice.

### API
- `PUT /v1/cart/items/{sku}` body `{ "quantity": 2 }`; `GET /v1/cart`
- `POST /v1/checkouts` with `Idempotency-Key` header, body address, shipping option, payment token; returns `202` with order id and status when payment is asynchronous, or `201` if it completed in time
- `GET /v1/orders/{id}` and `GET /v1/orders?cursor=...`
- `GET /v1/search?q=...&brand=...&sort=price` (cursor or search-after pagination)

### Data model (core tables)
- `products`(id, title, description, seller_id, price, attrs), `inventory`(sku, available, reserved), `reservations`(id, order_id, sku, qty, expires_at, status).
- `orders`(id, user_id, status, total, currency, idempotency_key unique per user, version, created_at), `order_lines`(order_id, sku, qty, unit_price) with the price copied at order time.
- `idempotency_keys`(key, user_id, request_hash, response, created_at), `payments`(id, order_id, provider_ref, status).
- Shard orders by user id so "my orders" is a single shard query; admin and reporting queries go to a replica or a warehouse.

### Scaling and failure handling
- Stateless services scale horizontally behind the gateway; the browse path scales with caches and replicas, the checkout path scales by separating hot SKUs and sharding orders.
- Isolate the flash sale: give checkout and inventory their own capacity and rate limits so a surge on a few products cannot starve browsing. Shed load early with a waiting room and a clear "sold out" response.
- Payment provider down: stop accepting new checkouts for that method with a clear message, keep carts, and retry unknown payments. Use a circuit breaker and timeouts on every outbound call.
- Event bus down: write events to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order and publish from there, so no event is lost and none is published for a rolled-back order.
- Monitor: checkout success rate, payment unknown count and age, reservation expiry rate, oversell invariant (available below zero must be zero), search index lag, p99 latency per path, and per-SKU lock wait time.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **When to reserve stock.** At add-to-cart: simplest for users but carts hold stock hostage and abandoned carts hurt sales. At checkout start with a timeout (chosen here): a fair balance. At payment time only: no hostage stock but a customer can pay and then be told it is gone, which is the worst experience, unless you accept overselling and compensate (some retailers do, for low-value items).
- **Strong consistency for inventory, eventual for the catalog.** Money and stock need transactions; descriptions and search do not. Treating them differently is what makes the system both correct and fast.
- **Saga vs distributed transaction.** Two-phase commit across the inventory, order and payment systems is brittle and the payment provider cannot take part in it. A saga with compensations and idempotent steps is the practical choice.
- **Single database vs services.** A well-run modular monolith with one database can carry this load and avoids the saga entirely until the organisation or scale forces a split. Splitting early is a cost, not a goal.
- **Search: database full text vs a dedicated engine.** Database search is enough for a small catalog; at 50 million products with facets and ranking a dedicated engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr) is the usual choice, accepting extra infrastructure and index lag.
- **Not built here:** recommendations, reviews, promotions and coupons engine, tax and shipping rate calculation, multi-warehouse allocation, fraud scoring, returns, and multi-currency.

hld/social-media-feed.reference:
This is one reasonable design. The numbers are estimates to show the reasoning; adjust them and the conclusions follow.

### Capacity estimate
- Posts: 20 million per day / 86,400 s is about 230 posts/s on average. Assume peak is 3x, so about 700/s.
- Feed reads: 100 million users x 10 opens per day = 1 billion/day, about 12,000/s on average and 35,000/s at peak. The read:write ratio is roughly 50:1, so reads must be cheap.
- Fan-out on write for normal accounts: 230 posts/s x 200 followers is about 46,000 feed-entry writes/s on average, about 140,000/s at peak. That is high but fine for a sharded in-memory store fed by a queue.
- One celebrity post with 30 million followers would be 30 million writes in one burst. That one number is why pure push fails.
- Feed cache: store about 500 entries per active user, each a post id (8 bytes) and a score or timestamp (8 bytes), about 16 bytes: 500 x 16 B = 8 KB per user. For 100 million users that is about 800 GB, so a Redis (or similar) cluster of some tens of nodes with replicas.
- Post storage: 20 million posts/day x about 1 KB of metadata is about 20 GB/day, about 7 TB/year. Media is separate, in object storage behind a CDN.

### Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> GW[API gateway]
  GW --> PS[Post service]
  GW --> FS[Feed service]
  GW --> GS[Graph service: follows]
  PS --> PDB[(Post store, sharded by post id)]
  PS --> Q[[Fan-out queue]]
  Q --> FW[Fan-out workers]
  FW --> GS
  FW --> FC[(Feed cache: sorted list per user)]
  FS --> FC
  FS --> PC[(Post cache)]
  PC --> PDB
  FS --> CP[(Celebrity post lists)]
  FS --> RK[Ranking service]
  PS --> CP
```

**Write path.** The client posts to the post service. It stores the post (id from a time-ordered generator such as a Snowflake-style id, so ids sort by time), then publishes a small event to a queue and returns. Fan-out workers read the event, fetch the author's follower list from the graph service, and for each follower push the post id into that follower's feed list in the cache. Workers only push to followers who were active recently; inactive users get their feed rebuilt when they return.

**Celebrity problem (hybrid).** If an author has more than a threshold of followers (say 100,000), the post is not fanned out. It is only written to the author's own post list. When a user opens their feed, the feed service reads the precomputed feed (pushed posts from normal accounts) and merges in recent posts from the few celebrities that user follows (pulled at read time, from a cached list per celebrity). A user follows only a handful of celebrities, so the merge is cheap and the celebrity list is one of the hottest cache keys, which caches well.

**Read path.** The feed service reads the first page of ids from the user's feed list, merges celebrity posts, optionally calls ranking, then hydrates ids into full posts using a post cache (batch get; misses go to the post store), and adds counts and the author's profile data from their own caches. Hydration at read time means edits and deletes show up immediately and the feed list stays tiny.

### API
- `POST /v1/posts` body `{ "text": "...", "mediaIds": ["m1"] }` returns `201` with the post.
- `GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=<opaque>` returns `{ "items": [...], "nextCursor": "..." }`.
- `GET /v1/users/{id}/posts?limit=20&cursor=...`
- `PUT /v1/users/{id}/follow` and `DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow`.

**Pagination.** Use a cursor, not an offset. The cursor encodes the position, for example the (score, post id) of the last item returned. With offset, a new post pushed to the top shifts everything and the next page repeats an item. A cursor says "items older than this", so new posts do not disturb it. If ranking reorders items, snapshot the ranked candidate list for the session (or cache it for a short time keyed by a feed session id) so scrolling stays consistent.

### Data model
- `posts`: post_id (time-ordered), author_id, text, media refs, created_at. Sharded by post id (or by author id if you favour profile page locality; that creates hot shards for celebrities, so many teams shard by post id and keep a separate author index).
- `follows`: (follower_id, followee_id, created_at), stored twice, indexed by follower and by followee, in a store sharded by the indexed user, because you need both "who do I follow" and "who follows me".
- `feed:{user_id}`: a sorted collection of (post_id, score), capped to about 500 entries by trimming the oldest.
- `counters`: likes and comments counts, updated asynchronously and cached, since exact real-time counts are not required.

### Ranking
Start with reverse chronological: it is predictable, cheap and easy to explain. When ranking is added, do it in two stages: candidate generation (the merged feed list, a few hundred ids) and then a scoring step using features such as author affinity, post age, engagement so far, and media type, producing a score by a model or weighted formula. Keep the model behind the ranking service interface with a timeout and fall back to chronological order if it is slow or down.

### Scaling and failure handling
- The queue absorbs bursts; workers scale horizontally by partitioning on follower shard. Retries must be idempotent: adding the same post id to a sorted set twice changes nothing.
- Feed cache loss: rebuild a user's feed on demand from the graph and the recent post lists (the pull path), which is the same code used for inactive users, so the fallback is exercised daily.
- Hot keys: a celebrity's post list and a viral post are read by millions. Replicate those keys, add a short local in-process cache in the feed service, and let CDN or edge caching serve the post media.
- Fan-out lag: if the queue backs up, feeds get fresher posts later but still load. Monitor queue age, not just depth.
- Deleted posts and blocked users: filter at hydration time, so no one has to scrub millions of lists.
- Monitor: feed p50/p99 latency, cache hit rate, fan-out queue age, post-to-visible delay, hydration miss rate, ranking timeout rate.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **Push vs pull vs hybrid.** Pure pull is simple and exact but makes each read do a heavy merge across hundreds of accounts. Pure push makes reads fast but multiplies writes and fails on celebrities. The hybrid costs more code and a threshold to tune, in return for both fast reads and bounded writes. The threshold is a tunable, not a law.
- **Store the feed as ids, not copies of posts.** Storage is tiny and edits are consistent, but each read pays for hydration. Storing full posts in the feed would remove that cost and make every edit a massive rewrite.
- **Cache only active users.** Saves memory but a returning user's first load is slower. Another option is a longer retention for more users at a higher cost.
- **Eventual consistency.** A user may not see their own post at once in their own feed unless you insert it into their own list synchronously (cheap and worth doing).
- **Not built here:** ads insertion, stories, spam and abuse filtering, real-time push of new posts to open feeds (a websocket or "new posts" banner), and a full recommendation system for posts from accounts the user does not follow.

lld/food-delivery.reference:
This is one reasonable design, not the only valid one. The alternatives are named where they matter.

### Classes
- `Restaurant` owns a `Menu`, a list of `MenuItem` (id, name, price as `Money`, available).
- `Customer` and `DeliveryPartner` (id, location, status: AVAILABLE, ASSIGNED, OFFLINE).
- `Order` is the aggregate: customer, restaurant, a list of `OrderLine` (item name, unit price copied at order time, quantity), a status, an optional partner, and a price breakdown. It enforces its own state transitions.
- `OrderService` is the facade used by the API: `place`, `accept`, `markReady`, `cancel`, `deliver`.
- `PricingEngine` applies an ordered list of `PricingRule` objects (strategy). Rules: `DeliveryFeeRule`, `PercentageDiscount`, `FlatDiscount`, `FreeDeliveryAbove`.
- `PartnerAssigner` (strategy interface) with `NearestPartnerAssigner`; a `PartnerPool` holds the partners and does the atomic claim.
- `OrderEventListener` (observer) with `NotificationListener`; `OrderService` publishes an event on every transition.

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class OrderService {
    +place(customer, restaurant, items) Order
    +accept(orderId)
    +markReady(orderId)
    +cancel(orderId)
    +deliver(orderId)
  }
  class Order {
    id
    status
    lines
    breakdown
    +transitionTo(newStatus)
  }
  class OrderLine {
    itemName
    unitPrice
    quantity
  }
  class OrderStatus {
    <<enumeration>>
    PLACED
    ACCEPTED
    PREPARING
    READY
    PICKED_UP
    DELIVERED
    CANCELLED
    REJECTED
  }
  class Restaurant {
    menu
    +isOpen() bool
  }
  class MenuItem {
    name
    price
    available
  }
  class Customer
  class DeliveryPartner {
    location
    status
  }
  class PricingEngine {
    +price(lines, rules) PriceBreakdown
  }
  class PricingRule {
    <<interface>>
    +apply(running) Money
  }
  class PartnerAssigner {
    <<interface>>
    +assign(order, pool) DeliveryPartner
  }
  class PartnerPool {
    +tryClaim(partnerId) bool
    +release(partnerId)
  }
  class OrderEventListener {
    <<interface>>
    +onEvent(order, from, to)
  }
  OrderService --> Order
  OrderService --> PricingEngine
  OrderService --> PartnerAssigner
  OrderService --> OrderEventListener
  Order *-- OrderLine
  Order --> OrderStatus
  Order --> Customer
  Order --> Restaurant
  Order --> DeliveryPartner
  Restaurant o-- MenuItem
  PricingEngine o-- PricingRule
  PricingRule <|.. PercentageDiscount
  PricingRule <|.. FlatDiscount
  PricingRule <|.. DeliveryFeeRule
  PartnerAssigner <|.. NearestPartnerAssigner
  NearestPartnerAssigner --> PartnerPool
  OrderEventListener <|.. NotificationListener
```

### Order state machine
PLACED -> ACCEPTED (restaurant) -> PREPARING (restaurant) -> READY (restaurant) -> PICKED_UP (partner) -> DELIVERED (partner).
PLACED -> REJECTED (restaurant, or timeout). PLACED, ACCEPTED -> CANCELLED (customer); PREPARING -> CANCELLED only by the restaurant or support, with a cancellation fee. After PICKED_UP there is no cancellation, only a refund process outside this model.

`Order.transitionTo` looks the move up in a table `Map<OrderStatus, Set<OrderStatus>>` and throws on an illegal one. That keeps every rule in one place and gives the unit test a single table to cover.

### Pricing as a strategy pipeline
`PricingEngine` starts from the sum of `unitPrice * quantity` and passes the running amount through each rule in a defined order (discounts first, then fees, then tax, for example). Order matters: a 10% discount before the delivery fee is not the same as after it, so the order is part of the contract and is tested. The breakdown (subtotal, discounts, fee, total) is stored on the order so it can be shown and audited without recomputing. Money is an integer number of minor units, never a float.

### Assignment and concurrency
`NearestPartnerAssigner` ranks available partners by distance and tries to `tryClaim` the best one. `tryClaim` is an atomic compare-and-set from AVAILABLE to ASSIGNED (a lock per partner, a CAS on the status, or a conditional UPDATE in a database). If the claim fails because another order got there first, it tries the next candidate. If nobody is free the order stays READY and is retried by a timer. If the partner declines or times out, the partner is released and the assigner runs again with that partner excluded.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **State machine: table vs State pattern.** A transition table is the smallest thing that works and is easy to test. One class per state is worthwhile when each state has significant different behaviour (for example, different cancellation fees and side effects). With about eight states and little per-state behaviour, the table is usually enough; the State pattern is the reasonable choice if behaviour grows.
- **Price snapshot vs live reference.** Copying the price onto the order line costs a little duplication but protects history. The alternative, versioned menu items, is heavier and only pays off if you also need menu history for other reasons.
- **Discounts: strategy list vs decorator vs chain of responsibility.** A list of rules is simplest. Decorators suit stacking where each wraps the next; a chain suits rules that can stop the pipeline (for example an exclusive coupon). Pick based on whether rules interact.
- **Assign at accept time or at ready time.** Assigning early cuts waiting but may leave the partner idle at the restaurant; assigning late reduces idle time but may delay pickup. Real systems often assign when the estimated preparation time is close to the travel time.
- **Push to one partner vs offer to several.** Offering to one partner at a time is simple and avoids conflicts; broadcasting to a few and taking the first accept is faster but needs the atomic claim above.
- **Events: synchronous observers vs a message queue.** In-process listeners are fine for this exercise; in production notifications go through a queue so a slow SMS provider cannot slow down a state change.
- **Out of scope but worth naming:** batching several orders per partner, surge pricing, refunds, restaurant opening hours, and persisting the order with optimistic locking (a version column) so two concurrent transitions cannot both succeed.

lld/movie-ticket-booking.reference:
This is one reasonable design. Where a decision has a reasonable alternative, it is named below.

### Classes
- `Theatre` owns `Screen`s; `Screen` owns `Seat`s (row, number, category). These are static layout data.
- `Movie` and `Show` (movie, screen, start time, price per category). `Show` is the unit of consistency: it owns the seat inventory for that show.
- `ShowSeats` (inside `Show`) maps seat id to a state: AVAILABLE, HELD (hold id, expiry) or BOOKED (booking id).
- `SeatHold` (id, user, show, seats, expiresAt, status).
- `Booking` (id, user, show, seats, amount, status: CONFIRMED, CANCELLED, payment reference).
- `BookingService` is the facade: `hold`, `confirm`, `cancel`, `expireHolds`.
- `PaymentGateway` (interface) with an adapter per provider; `PricingStrategy` (interface) so a matinee or a member discount is a new class.
- `Clock` (interface) injected so expiry can be tested without sleeping.

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class BookingService {
    +hold(userId, showId, seatIds) SeatHold
    +confirm(holdId, paymentToken) Booking
    +cancel(bookingId)
    +expireHolds()
  }
  class Theatre
  class Screen
  class Seat {
    row
    number
    category
  }
  class Movie
  class Show {
    startTime
    +tryHold(seatIds, holdId, expiresAt) bool
    +book(seatIds, holdId, bookingId) bool
    +release(holdId)
    +freeSeats() list
  }
  class SeatState {
    <<enumeration>>
    AVAILABLE
    HELD
    BOOKED
  }
  class SeatHold {
    id
    userId
    seatIds
    expiresAt
    status
  }
  class Booking {
    id
    seatIds
    amount
    status
  }
  class PaymentGateway {
    <<interface>>
    +charge(amount, token, idempotencyKey) PaymentResult
    +refund(paymentRef)
  }
  class PricingStrategy {
    <<interface>>
    +price(show, seats) Money
  }
  class Clock {
    <<interface>>
    +now() Instant
  }
  Theatre o-- Screen
  Screen o-- Seat
  Show --> Movie
  Show --> Screen
  Show --> SeatState
  BookingService --> Show
  BookingService --> SeatHold
  BookingService --> Booking
  BookingService --> PaymentGateway
  BookingService --> PricingStrategy
  BookingService --> Clock
  Booking --> Show
```

### Seat state machine
AVAILABLE -> HELD when a user selects the seat (only if every requested seat is AVAILABLE, or HELD with an expiry already in the past).
HELD -> BOOKED when the owner of the hold confirms with a successful payment before expiry.
HELD -> AVAILABLE when the owner releases, payment fails, or the hold expires.
BOOKED -> AVAILABLE only through cancellation.

### All-or-nothing and concurrency
`Show.tryHold` runs under a lock owned by that show (a mutex in one process, or a database row lock or conditional update in a real system): it checks that every requested seat is free, and only then marks all of them HELD. Checking and marking one seat at a time would let two overlapping requests each take part of the set. One lock per show means a popular show serialises its own bookings but never blocks other shows.

Expiry has two layers: a seat whose hold has expired is treated as available when read (lazy), and a periodic `expireHolds` sweep (or a delayed job, or a Redis key TTL) frees them and keeps the free-seat listing cheap (active).

### Payment ordering and failures
1. `hold`: seats become HELD for N minutes. Return the hold id and the expiry to the client.
2. `confirm`: re-check that the hold still exists, belongs to the user and has not expired.
3. Charge using the hold id as the idempotency key, so a retry cannot charge twice.
4. On success, call `Show.book`, which moves the seats to BOOKED only if they are still held by this hold, and create the booking.
5. On failure, release the hold.

Failure cases. Payment fails: release the hold. The charge times out with an unknown result: keep the seats held a little longer and ask the gateway for the status using the idempotency key, rather than guessing. Payment succeeds but the hold already expired and another user took the seats: refund automatically and tell the user; to make this rare, add a short grace period or extend the hold when a payment starts. The booking write fails after a successful charge: a retry with the same key is safe, and a reconciliation job compares gateway charges with bookings.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **Lock per show vs per seat.** One lock per show is simple and enough for hundreds of seats. Per-seat locks give more parallelism but need ordered acquisition to avoid deadlock; they rarely matter at this size.
- **Pessimistic lock vs optimistic version check.** In a database, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the show's seat rows, or a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'AVAILABLE'` that checks the affected row count, are both reasonable. Optimistic retries are cheap when conflicts are rare but wasteful for a hot release of a blockbuster.
- **Hold in memory vs in Redis vs in the database.** In memory is fine for the exercise; with several servers the hold must be shared, so Redis with a TTL, or a row with an `expires_at` column, is typical. The database as the source of truth is the safest; Redis is faster but needs care about losing holds on failover.
- **Seat status on the Seat vs per show.** A boolean on `Seat` links the 7 pm and 9 pm shows incorrectly; keep state per (show, seat).
- **Lazy vs active expiry.** Lazy alone is correct but leaves stale counts; active alone can lag and allow a short window where a seat looks held. Using both is cheap.
- **Out of scope but worth naming:** waiting rooms for very hot releases, group bookings that must be adjacent, seat maps with best-available selection, and refunds policy by time before the show.
